sectionToMerge.h2: Frequently Asked Questions About Radium-223 Dichloride (Xofigo) for Bone Metastases
sectionToMerge.intro: These FAQs explain how Radium-223 dichloride (Xofigo) is used to treat bone metastases, who may be eligible, and what patients and caregivers should know about safety, cost, and access.

items.a: Radium-223 dichloride, sold as Xofigo, is a radioactive medicine used to treat cancer that has spread to the bones. It is an alpha-particle emitter that mimics calcium and settles in areas of active bone growth, where metastases are usually most concentrated. It is given by injection and is mainly approved for prostate cancer that no longer responds to hormone therapy. A qualified oncology team decides whether it is appropriate.

items.q: How does Radium-223 work against bone metastases?
items.a: Radium-223 works by delivering targeted radiation directly to bone metastases. Because it behaves like calcium, it collects in areas where cancer is actively damaging bone, then releases short-range alpha particles that kill nearby cancer cells while limiting harm to surrounding healthy tissue and bone marrow. This targeted action may help reduce bone pain and slow disease progression, though individual results depend on cancer type, extent of spread, and overall health.

items.q: Which cancers is Radium-223 used for?
items.a: Radium-223 is mainly approved for men with castration-resistant prostate cancer that has spread to the bones and is causing symptoms, without known spread to internal organs. It is not routinely used for cancers that have spread to soft tissues or organs such as the liver or lungs. Its use in other cancers is investigational. Whether it suits a particular patient depends on diagnosis, imaging, previous treatment, and specialist review.

items.q: How is Radium-223 different from other bone-targeted treatments?
items.a: Radium-223 differs from drugs like bisphosphonates or denosumab because it actively delivers radiation to kill cancer cells in bone, rather than only strengthening bone or reducing fractures. Unlike external beam radiation, it treats multiple bone sites at once through a single injection. It may be used alongside bone-supportive medicines, but the combination and sequence should be discussed with the treating oncology team based on each patient's situation.

items.q: Who is eligible for Radium-223 therapy?
items.a: Radium-223 may be considered for men with castration-resistant prostate cancer that has spread to the bones and is causing symptoms, with no known spread to internal organs. Eligibility depends on cancer type, imaging findings, blood counts, previous treatment, and overall health. Patients with adequate bone marrow function are generally preferred. Final suitability is decided by the treating oncology team after reviewing scans, pathology, and laboratory results.

Radium-223 is given as a slow injection into a vein, usually once every four weeks for up to six doses. Each session is short and done as an outpatient procedure in a nuclear medicine or oncology unit. Blood counts are checked before each dose to confirm the patient can safely continue. The exact schedule and number of doses may be adjusted by the treating team based on response and side effects.

items.q: What are the common side effects of Radium-223?
items.a: Common side effects of Radium-223 may include nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, and swelling of the legs, along with lowered blood counts such as anemia or reduced platelets. Because it targets bone, it can affect the bone marrow, so regular blood tests are needed. Most side effects are manageable, but severity varies between patients. Any new or worsening symptoms should be discussed promptly with the treating oncology team.

items.q: Is Radium-223 safe for family members and caregivers?
items.a: Radium-223 is generally considered safe for people around the patient when simple precautions are followed. It emits short-range alpha radiation that does not travel far, so normal contact is usually fine. Because the medicine is cleared mainly through stool, patients are advised to follow hygiene guidance around the toilet for a short period after each dose. The nuclear medicine team provides specific safety instructions for each patient's situation.

items.q: How much does Radium-223 treatment cost?
items.a: The cost of Radium-223 varies widely and depends on the country, hospital, number of doses, and supportive care needed. A full course involves up to six injections, so total cost reflects the complete schedule rather than a single dose. Final pricing also depends on scans, blood tests, consultations, and any complications. Patients should request a written estimate from the treating hospital, as costs are not fixed and cannot be guaranteed.

Radium-223 may be available at selected nuclear medicine and cancer centers in India, though availability can change and is not uniform across hospitals. Because it is a specialized radiopharmaceutical, it is offered mainly at centers with the required licensing and facilities. Patients should confirm current availability, scheduling, and estimated cost directly with the hospital. Whether it is suitable in a specific case depends on diagnosis, imaging, and specialist review.

Radium-223 is available in several countries with established nuclear medicine programs, including parts of North America, Europe, and Asia. Availability depends on regulatory approval, supply, and whether a center is licensed to handle radiopharmaceuticals. Because access and scheduling differ by location, patients considering treatment abroad should verify current availability and estimated cost with each hospital. Treatment access ultimately depends on hospital acceptance and medical review of the patient's records.

items.q: Can Radium-223 be combined with other prostate cancer treatments?
items.a: Radium-223 is sometimes used alongside other prostate cancer treatments, but combinations must be chosen carefully. Certain pairings, such as with some hormonal agents plus steroids, have raised safety concerns in studies and may increase the risk of fractures. It is often given with bone-supportive medicines. The right combination and sequence depend on the patient's treatment history and should be decided by the treating oncology team, not self-selected.

items.q: How is response to Radium-223 monitored?
items.a: Response to Radium-223 is monitored through symptoms, blood tests, and imaging over the course of treatment. Doctors may track bone pain, quality of life, and blood markers, and use scans to assess disease. Because Radium-223 targets bone, standard PSA readings alone may not reflect its full effect, so the treating team interprets results together. Monitoring helps decide whether to continue, pause, or adjust the planned doses.

items.q: Are there clinical trials involving Radium-223?
items.a: Yes, clinical trials continue to study Radium-223, including new combinations and its use in different disease settings. Trials may explore how it works with other therapies or its role at various stages of cancer. Eligibility is decided after medical record review and investigator assessment, and trials often have strict inclusion and exclusion criteria. Enrollment and benefit cannot be guaranteed, and participation should be discussed with the treating oncology team.

items.q: What medical reports are needed before starting Radium-223?
items.a: Before starting Radium-223, doctors usually need recent bone scans or other imaging, pathology confirming the cancer type, PSA and other blood test results, and a summary of previous treatments. A record of current medicines and overall health is also helpful. These reports allow the oncology team to confirm eligibility and plan safely. Gathering complete and up-to-date records makes review faster, especially for patients seeking treatment in another city or country.

items.q: How long does a full course of Radium-223 take?
items.a: A full course of Radium-223 typically spans several months, since injections are given about once every four weeks for up to six doses. Each visit itself is short, but blood tests before each dose and periodic reviews add to the overall timeline. International patients should plan for repeated visits or an extended stay, and confirm the expected schedule and follow-up arrangements with the treating hospital before travel.

items.q: Can Radium-223 treatment be repeated after completion?
items.a: Repeating Radium-223 after a completed course may be considered in selected patients, but it is not automatic. The decision depends on how the disease responded, current blood counts, bone marrow health, and other available treatment options. Re-treatment is only offered after careful specialist review and is not suitable for everyone. Whether another course is appropriate should be discussed thoroughly with the treating oncology team based on the patient's overall condition.

items.q: How does CancerFax help patients with Radium-223 therapy?
items.a: CancerFax helps patients organize medical reports, identify relevant specialists or treatment centers, estimate possible costs, and coordinate second opinions, appointments, travel, visa, and follow-up support. Treatment decisions are always made by the qualified oncology team after reviewing the patient's diagnosis, stage, biomarkers, previous treatment, and overall health. This support is meant to guide planning and does not guarantee hospital admission, treatment acceptance, or any specific outcome.
